title: Solar-Cycle Variation of Newly Emerging Coronal Holes during Solar Cycle 24
summary: Coronal holes (CHs) are regions of predominantly open magnetic field and important sources of high-speed solar wind streams. We present a manually compiled catalogue of newly emerging CHs during Solar Cycle 24 (2010-2019), identified from daily CHIMERA maps provided by SolarMonitor. Unlike existing area-based catalogues, our dataset tracks the daily emergence of new CHs in northern, southern, and equatorial latitude zones. The emergence rate of equatorial CHs is anti-correlated with the International Sunspot Number (Pearson r = -0.523, p = 6.2 x 10^-9), indicating reduced formation of low-latitude CHs near solar maximum. The hemispheric asymmetry of CH emergence is also anti-correlated with the hemispheric asymmetry of sunspot activity (r = -0.461, p = 5.2 x 10^-7), suggesting that new CHs preferentially emerge in the hemisphere with lower sunspot activity. The total CH emergence rate is lowest near solar maximum and highest during the declining phase. These results provide new observational constraints on the evolution of open magnetic flux over the solar cycle.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a manually compiled catalogue of newly emerging coronal holes (CHs) during Solar Cycle 24 (2010-2019), tracking their daily emergence across northern, southern, and equatorial latitude zones. Key findings include: equatorial CH emergence anti-correlates with sunspot number, hemispheric CH emergence asymmetry anti-correlates with sunspot hemispheric asymmetry, and total CH emergence is lowest near solar maximum and highest during the declining phase.
AI.motivation: Existing CH catalogues are area-based and do not track the daily emergence of new coronal holes. This work aims to provide a new observational dataset that tracks CH emergence events in different latitude zones to better understand the evolution of open magnetic flux over the solar cycle.
AI.method: Daily CHIMERA maps from SolarMonitor were used to manually compile a catalogue of newly emerging coronal holes during Solar Cycle 24 (2010-2019). CH emergence was tracked in northern, southern, and equatorial latitude zones, and correlations were computed against sunspot number and hemispheric sunspot asymmetry.
AI.result: Equatorial CH emergence rate is anti-correlated with International Sunspot Number (r = -0.523, p = 6.2 x 10^-9). Hemispheric asymmetry of CH emergence anti-correlates with hemispheric sunspot asymmetry (r = -0.461, p = 5.2 x 10^-7), indicating CHs preferentially emerge in the hemisphere with lower sunspot activity. Total CH emergence rate is lowest near solar maximum and highest during the declining phase.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide new observational constraints on the evolution of open magnetic flux over the solar cycle, revealing that CH emergence is suppressed near solar maximum and enhanced during the declining phase, with hemispheric preferences that oppose sunspot activity.

title: Agentic Active Learning Meets Visual Embeddings: Finding Anomalies among 370 000 Variable Stars from ASAS-SN
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: Unusual light-curve morphologies can point to rare physical configurations or new phenomena, but automatic searches for anomalies are often dominated by artifacts. Separating genuine anomalies from false positives has traditionally required manual vetting, which does not scale to modern surveys. We present an active learning framework for detecting anomalies in samples of periodic variable stars, with the vetting delegated to multimodal large language model agents. The initial ranking comes from isolation forests trained on DINOv2 ViT-g/14 embeddings of phase-folded light curves. The agents iteratively review the light-curve images of the top-ranked candidates and assign relevance scores, which are propagated through the embedding space to prioritize the next targets. A logistic regression step then extends the search beyond label propagation, and a multi-agent consensus review filters false positives. Using Gemini~3 Flash agents, we applied the pipeline to $373\,646$ periodic variables from ASAS-SN Sky Patrol V2.0. Across $51$ iterations, the agents labeled ${\sim}1\%$ of the sample in roughly $3$ hours at a cost of ${\approx}$ $$40$, yielding our final catalog of $24$ anomalies ($18$ newly reported) and $153$ potentially interesting objects. The anomalies include eclipsing binaries with extremely deep primary eclipses, high-amplitude contact binaries and pulsators, and a symbiotic nova in outburst for over two decades. At the same labeling budget, the initial ranking would have recovered only $30\%$ of our catalog, while reaching its lowest-ranked anomaly would have required ${\sim}70$ times the budget. These results demonstrate the feasibility of agentic active learning for anomaly detection in existing and upcoming photometric surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an active learning framework for detecting anomalies in periodic variable stars, where vetting is delegated to multimodal large language model (LLM) agents. The pipeline uses isolation forests on DINOv2 embeddings of phase-folded light curves for initial ranking, iteratively reviews top candidates with Gemini 3 Flash agents, propagates relevance scores through the embedding space, and applies multi-agent consensus review. Applied to 373,646 periodic variables from ASAS-SN, it labeled ~1% of the sample in ~3 hours at ~$40 cost, producing 24 anomalies (18 newly reported) and 153 interesting objects, outperforming the initial ranking by ~70x in budget efficiency.
AI.motivation: Automatic searches for anomalous light-curve morphologies are often dominated by artifacts, and separating genuine anomalies from false positives has traditionally required manual vetting that does not scale to modern surveys. The authors aim to overcome this scalability bottleneck by delegating the vetting process to multimodal LLM agents within an active learning loop.
AI.method: The pipeline begins with isolation forests trained on DINOv2 ViT-g/14 embeddings of phase-folded light curves to produce an initial anomaly ranking. Multimodal LLM agents iteratively review the top-ranked light-curve images and assign relevance scores, which are propagated through the embedding space via label propagation to prioritize subsequent targets. A logistic regression step extends the search beyond label propagation, and a multi-agent consensus review filters out false positives.
AI.result: Applied to 373,646 periodic variables from ASAS-SN Sky Patrol V2.0 using Gemini 3 Flash agents across 51 iterations, the pipeline labeled ~1% of the sample in roughly 3 hours at a cost of ~$40, yielding 24 anomalies (18 newly reported) and 153 potentially interesting objects. Anomalies include eclipsing binaries with extremely deep primary eclipses, high-amplitude contact binaries and pulsators, and a symbiotic nova in outburst for over two decades. At the same labeling budget, the initial ranking alone would have recovered only 30% of the catalog, and recovering its lowest-ranked anomaly would have required ~70x the budget.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of agentic active learning for anomaly detection in existing and upcoming photometric surveys, showing that LLM-agent-driven vetting within an active learning loop can significantly reduce labeling costs while substantially outperforming static ranking methods.

title: A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic giant branch star Mira A
summary: Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained. However, recent observations show massive directional mass ejections from the nearby asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star Mira~A that appear not to be driven by radiation pressure on the dust. We observationally investigate whether magnetic fields are responsible for the mass loss ejections from Mira A. We obtained full-polarisation ALMA observations of the SiO $v=1$, $J=5\rightarrow4$ maser transition at 215 GHz with angular resolutions of 1.5-2.6 au. The observations reveal a highly magnetized loop-like mass ejection traced by strongly polarised SiO masers extending to approximately eight stellar radii. The morphology, polarisation pattern, energetics, and kinematics indicate a magnetically driven eruption analogous to a stellar coronal mass ejection. The observations demonstrate that magnetic eruptions can dominate mass loss from evolved stars and imply that magnetic fields must become an integral component of future models of AGB, and potentially other cool giant, winds.

AI.tldr: ALMA full-polarisation observations of SiO masers around Mira A reveal a highly magnetized, loop-like mass ejection extending to ~8 stellar radii, indicating a magnetic eruption analogous to a stellar coronal mass ejection—demonstrating that magnetic eruptions can dominate mass loss from evolved stars and must be included in AGB wind models.
AI.motivation: Traditional models attribute mass loss from low- and intermediate-mass evolved stars to dust-driven winds, but recent observations of massive directional ejections from Mira A appear inconsistent with radiation pressure on dust. The influence of magnetic fields on such mass loss remains poorly constrained, motivating an observational investigation into magnetic field-driven mechanisms.
AI.method: Full-polarisation ALMA observations of the SiO v=1, J=5→4 maser transition at 215 GHz with angular resolutions of 1.5–2.6 au were obtained to probe the magnetic field structure and kinematics of the mass ejection from the AGB star Mira A.
AI.result: The observations reveal a highly magnetized loop-like mass ejection traced by strongly polarised SiO masers extending to approximately eight stellar radii. The morphology, polarisation pattern, energetics, and kinematics indicate a magnetically driven eruption analogous to a stellar coronal mass ejection.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic eruptions can dominate mass loss from evolved stars, and magnetic fields must become an integral component of future models of AGB and potentially other cool giant winds.

title: Periodic activity on the (sub)mm surface of the AGB star Mira A
comment: Submitted to A&A, with most comments from the 1st round of review implemented
summary: Evolved stars on the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) lose mass through stellar winds launched from their dynamic extended atmospheres. Recent high-angular-resolution observations of the archetypal AGB star Mira A (o Ceti) have revealed compact hotspots on its submillimetre (submm) surface, whose origin remains unclear. We aim to characterise the submm photosphere of Mira A and investigate the properties and temporal behaviour of the compact hotspots detected on its surface. We analysed 19 epochs of high-angular-resolution observations obtained with the Atacama Large Millimetre/submillimetre Array in Bands 4, 6, 7, and 9, ranging from 134.34 to 669.25 GHz. The complex visibilities were fitted with parametric models to derive the flux density, size, morphology, and brightness temperature of the stellar disc and an additional more compact component across multiple pulsation phases and observing frequencies.Our results show that the flux density of the stellar disc increases with frequency while its apparent size decreases, in agreement with the expected stratified radio photosphere. In Band 6, both the flux density and the size of the stellar disc vary with pulsation phase, reaching maximum values close to optical maximum light and decreasing toward minimum light. Compact hotspots are detected in Bands~6 and 7 near maximum light, with their brightness temperatures exceeding those of the stellar disc by several thousand kelvins, reaching T>8600 K in Band 6. They are highly energetic and persist on timescales of weeks but evolve over longer timescales, showing changes in both position and intensity. Hotspot activity appears to occur repeatedly across multiple pulsation cycles and may be linked to strong shocks, magnetic activity, and/or episodic mass ejections, and could therefore play an important role in the mass-loss process in AGB stars.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 19 epochs of ALMA high-resolution observations (134–669 GHz) of the AGB star Mira A to characterize its submillimetre photosphere and the compact hotspots detected on its surface. The stellar disc shows frequency-dependent flux and size (stratified radio photosphere), with pulsation-phase-dependent variations in Band 6. Compact hotspots, detected in Bands 6 and 7 near optical maximum, have brightness temperatures exceeding 8600 K, persist for weeks but evolve over longer timescales, and may be linked to shocks, magnetic activity, or episodic mass ejections, potentially playing a role in AGB mass loss.
AI.motivation: The origin of compact hotspots observed on the submillimetre surface of the archetypal AGB star Mira A remains unclear, motivating a systematic characterization of the submm photosphere and the temporal/spectral behaviour of these hotspots across multiple pulsation phases and observing frequencies.
AI.method: Nineteen epochs of high-angular-resolution ALMA observations in Bands 4, 6, 7, and 9 (134.34–669.25 GHz) were analyzed. Complex visibilities were fitted with parametric models to derive flux density, size, morphology, and brightness temperature of the stellar disc plus an additional compact component across multiple pulsation phases and frequencies.
AI.result: The stellar disc flux increases with frequency while its apparent size decreases, consistent with a stratified radio photosphere. In Band 6, flux and size vary with pulsation phase, peaking near optical maximum. Compact hotspots appear in Bands 6 and 7 near maximum light with brightness temperatures exceeding those of the disc by thousands of kelvins (T>8600 K). They persist for weeks but evolve in position and intensity over longer timescales, recurring across multiple pulsation cycles.
AI.conclusion: The hotspots are highly energetic and recurrent, likely associated with strong shocks, magnetic activity, and/or episodic mass ejections, and may play an important role in the mass-loss process of AGB stars.

title: Flare waiting time as a novel proxy of stellar magnetic activity
comment: Science China Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy accepted
summary: Stellar flares have long served as stellar magnetic activity tracers. The flare waiting time, defined as the interval between two consecutive flares, provides a valuable diagnostic for probing underlying mechanisms of energy storage and release in stellar atmospheres. In this work, utilizing flaring M dwarfs observed by the Kepler satellite, we establish a simple yet effective activity proxy, i.e., median flare waiting time ($t_{\rm{w, med}}$). Our results show that the $t_{\rm{w, med}}$ can trace long-term activity levels similar to the flare rate. However, $t_{\rm{w, med}}$ corresponding to different waiting time percentiles may encode richer physical insights than flare rate. In addition, for the first time we construct a clear relation between $t_{\rm{w, med}}$ and stellar rotation period, which is quite similar to the canonical activity--rotation relation. More intriguingly, this relation exhibits a more notable supersaturation effect (i.e., below a critical rotation period, $t_{\rm{w, med}}$ begins to increase instead of keeping constant) compared to other activity proxies. The filling factor--rotation period relation favors poleward migration of active regions as the explanation for supersaturation, rather than coronal stripping. With the dramatic increase in stellar flares detected by missions like TESS and the upcoming Earth 2.0 satellite, $t_{\rm{w, med}}$ will become a powerful diagnostic for probing stellar magnetic activity and underlying physics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes median flare waiting time (t_w,med) as a new stellar magnetic activity proxy using Kepler observations of flaring M dwarfs, demonstrating it traces long-term activity levels comparable to flare rate while offering richer physical insights. It establishes for the first time a relation between t_w,med and stellar rotation period resembling the canonical activity-rotation relation, with a more pronounced supersaturation effect. The filling factor-rotation period relation supports poleward migration of active regions as the explanation for supersaturation rather than coronal stripping.
AI.motivation: Stellar flares serve as magnetic activity tracers, and flare waiting time provides a diagnostic for probing energy storage and release mechanisms in stellar atmospheres. The authors aim to establish a simple and effective activity proxy based on flare waiting times that can complement or improve upon existing proxies like flare rate.
AI.method: Using flaring M dwarfs observed by the Kepler satellite, the authors establish the median flare waiting time (t_w,med) as an activity proxy. They compare it with flare rate, investigate its behavior with respect to different waiting time percentiles, and construct relations between t_w,med and stellar rotation period. They also analyze the filling factor-rotation period relation to test competing explanations for supersaturation.
AI.result: The t_w,med traces long-term activity levels similarly to flare rate but encodes richer physical insights when considering different waiting time percentiles. A clear relation between t_w,med and stellar rotation period is established for the first time, resembling the canonical activity-rotation relation but exhibiting a more notable supersaturation effect. The filling factor analysis favors poleward migration of active regions over coronal stripping as the supersaturation mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Median flare waiting time is a powerful and promising stellar magnetic activity diagnostic. With increasing flare detections from TESS and the upcoming Earth 2.0 mission, t_w,med will become a valuable tool for probing stellar magnetic activity and the underlying physical mechanisms.

title: Fourier Morphology Diagnostics of Delta Cephei MESA-RSP Light Curves
summary: Fourier morphology provides a compact test of whether a nonlinear Cepheid model reproduces the observed harmonic content and asymmetric light-curve shape, not only the pulsation period. We apply Fourier and time-domain morphology diagnostics to observed and synthetic Delta Cephei light curves. The observed Johnson V-band light curve is represented by a Fourier template and compared with MIST bolometric-correction V-band light curves generated from the calibrated MESA-RSP model sequence. This study is framed as a target-specific morphology assessment rather than as a new Fourier-decomposition method. The observed template has Delta V = 0.8390 mag, R21 = 0.3401, R31 = 0.1943, rise fraction = 0.2775, and asymmetry index = 0.4450. The final accepted model, with RSP_alfam = 0.400 and RSP_alfat = 0.095, gives Delta V_syn = 0.0367 mag, R21 = 0.0185, R31 = 0.0028, rise fraction = 0.4860, and asymmetry index = 0.0280. The accepted calibration sequence therefore improves the synthetic amplitude only modestly and leaves the synthetic curve much too sinusoidal. The result shows that the accepted sequence is period-calibrated and morphology-tested, but it is not yet an observed-amplitude solution for Delta Cephei.

AI.tldr: This paper uses Fourier morphology (harmonic amplitudes and asymmetry metrics) to test whether a nonlinear Cepheid model reproduces not just the period but also the harmonic content and asymmetric light-curve shape of Delta Cephei. The accepted MESA-RSP calibration sequence reproduces the period and basic morphology but yields a synthetic light curve far too sinusoidal, with a much smaller amplitude than observed.
AI.motivation: To assess whether a calibrated nonlinear Cepheid model reproduces the observed harmonic structure and asymmetric light-curve shape of Delta Cephei—not merely its pulsation period—by applying Fourier and time-domain morphology diagnostics to observed and synthetic V-band light curves.
AI.method: The observed Johnson V-band light curve is represented by a Fourier template and compared against MIST bolometric-correction V-band light curves from a calibrated MESA-RSP model sequence. Morphology metrics include amplitude (Delta V), Fourier amplitude ratios (R21, R31), rise fraction, and an asymmetry index. This is a target-specific morphology assessment, not a new Fourier-decomposition technique.
AI.result: The observed template has Delta V = 0.8390 mag, R21 = 0.3401, R31 = 0.1943, rise fraction = 0.2775, asymmetry index = 0.4450. The accepted model (RSP_alfam = 0.400, RSP_alfat = 0.095) gives Delta V_syn = 0.0367 mag, R21 = 0.0185, R31 = 0.0028, rise fraction = 0.4860, asymmetry index = 0.0280—much lower in amplitude and far too sinusoidal compared to observations.
AI.conclusion: The accepted calibration sequence is period-calibrated and morphology-tested but does not yet provide an observed-amplitude solution for Delta Cephei. The synthetic light curve remains much too sinusoidal, indicating that further refinement is needed to match the observed harmonic content and asymmetric shape at the correct amplitude.

title: Evolutionary Period-Change Modeling of Delta Cephei with MESA Tracks
summary: Cepheid period changes provide a direct evolutionary diagnostic because the pulsation period responds to changes in stellar radius as a star crosses the instability strip. We present a controlled MESA evolutionary-track analysis for Delta Cephei using nonrotating, no-wind models. The period is estimated from the period-mean-density relation, P = Q [(R/Rsun)^3/(M/Msun)]^(1/2), with Q = 0.033 d. The adopted comparison values are P = 5.366531 d and dP/dt = -0.1006 s yr^-1. A solar-metallicity mass and overshoot grid identifies clean blueward solutions with negative dP/dt near the observed period, but the best such case has dP/dt = -0.6813 s yr^-1, a factor of 6.77 too large in magnitude. A metallicity pilot grid improves the result substantially, with a best clean-blueward model at M = 5.90 Msun, Z = 0.012, and fov,core = 0.010, giving P = 5.370677 d and dP/dt = -0.2460 s yr^-1. A local refinement around this solution does not improve beyond the same model. Thus, metallicity refinement reduces the period-change mismatch by a factor of about 2.77 relative to the solar-metallicity baseline, but the final nonrotating, no-wind, fixed-Q model still overpredicts the observed magnitude of dP/dt by a factor of about 2.45. The result supports a blueward evolutionary interpretation while identifying rotation, mass loss, binary-related effects, and structure-dependent pulsation periods as the natural scope of a follow-up study.

AI.tldr: This paper uses MESA evolutionary-track models for Delta Cephei (nonrotating, no-wind) to test whether blueward evolution explains its observed period change rate. Solar-metallicity models overpredict dP/dt by 6.77x, while metallicity refinement (Z=0.012) reduces the mismatch to 2.45x. The authors conclude the blueward interpretation is supported but that rotation, mass loss, binarity, and structure-dependent pulsation periods must be explored next.
AI.motivation: Cepheid period changes offer a direct evolutionary diagnostic since pulsation period responds to stellar radius changes as the star crosses the instability strip. The authors aim to reproduce Delta Cephei's observed period and period-change rate using controlled evolutionary models.
AI.method: MESA evolutionary tracks with nonrotating, no-wind models for Delta Cephei. The pulsation period is estimated from the period-mean-density relation P = Q[(R/Rsun)^3/(M/Msun)]^(1/2) with Q=0.033 d. A solar-metallicity mass and overshoot grid is explored, followed by a metallicity pilot grid and local refinement. Comparison values: P=5.366531 d, dP/dt=-0.1006 s yr^-1.
AI.result: Solar-metallicity grid yields a best blueward solution with dP/dt=-0.6813 s yr^-1 (6.77x too large). A metallicity pilot grid finds a best model at M=5.90 Msun, Z=0.012, fov,core=0.010 giving P=5.370677 d and dP/dt=-0.2460 s yr^-1, reducing the mismatch by ~2.77x. Local refinement does not improve beyond this model. The final model still overpredicts dP/dt magnitude by ~2.45x.
AI.conclusion: The blueward evolutionary interpretation of Delta Cephei's period change is supported, but the nonrotating, no-wind, fixed-Q assumption cannot fully reproduce the observed dP/dt. Follow-up work should incorporate rotation, mass loss, binary-related effects, and structure-dependent pulsation periods.

title: A quadratic balance relation for radial nonadiabatic pulsations
summary: Using a sesquilinear pressure - rate of volume change kernel and linear pulsation equations, we formulate a balance relation combining work integral, surface terms, norm integral and the real part of pulsation frequency (for $\exp({ωt})$ time dependence) in terms of linear radial pulsation variables. The resulting relation is exact within the adopted radial nonadiabatic formulation. We apply the quadratic balance relation to radial pulsations in AGB envelopes and use it to check the accuracy of computation and to obtain information about mode excitation and damping. We also compare the balance relation with the classical formulation based on dissipation and kinetic energy integrals and discuss the meaning of the components made explicit by the present decomposition that appear in our balance equation and their relevance for ordinary and strange modes in AGB envelopes.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exact quadratic balance relation for linear radial pulsations using a sesquilinear pressure-rate of volume change kernel, unifying work integral, surface terms, norm integral, and the real part of the pulsation frequency. It applies this to AGB stellar envelopes to verify computational accuracy and analyze mode excitation/damping, comparing with classical dissipation-based formulations and examining ordinary and strange modes.
AI.motivation: To provide an exact and more informative diagnostic tool for radial nonadiabatic pulsations in AGB envelopes, improving upon classical formulations (based on dissipation and kinetic energy integrals) to better assess computational accuracy and understand mode excitation/damping, particularly for distinguishing ordinary and strange modes.
AI.method: The authors formulate a quadratic balance relation using a sesquilinear pressure-rate of volume change kernel combined with linear radial pulsation equations. This relation exactly couples the work integral, surface terms, norm integral, and the real part of the pulsation frequency for exponential time dependence (exp(ωt)). The relation is applied to radial pulsations in AGB envelopes and compared against the classical dissipation/kinetic-energy based balance.
AI.result: The derived quadratic balance relation is exact within the adopted radial nonadiabatic formulation. It serves as a quantitative check on the accuracy of pulsation computations and provides decomposed components that clarify mode excitation, damping, and the nature of ordinary versus strange modes in AGB envelopes. Comparisons with classical formulations highlight the new insights made explicit by this decomposition.
AI.conclusion: The quadratic balance relation offers a rigorous and exact framework for validating and interpreting linear radial pulsation computations in AGB envelopes, with the decomposition revealing clearer physical meaning for mode excitation/damping and the distinction between ordinary and strange modes compared to the classical dissipation and kinetic energy approach.

title: The Interplay of Magnetic Fields, Turbulence and Vorticity in Core-Collapse Supernovae
comment: Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. D. 20 pages. 12 figures. Data behind figures available on zenodo
summary: The convective turbulent motion of the fluid below the shock in a core-collapse supernova stretches and amplifies the magnetic field of the progenitor star. The energy contained in the field is sourced from the work done by the fluid on the field which comes at the expense of the fluid's kinetic and internal energy. In addition to the energy exchange with the fluid, the magnetic field also has a back-reaction upon the fluid via a contribution to the baroclinic vector and thus affects the fluid vorticity. In this paper we explore the interaction of the magnetic field with the fluid in core-collapse supernovae using the ELEPHANT code with solar-metallicity stars of 15 and 20 \msun zero-age main sequence mass and purely toroidal initial magnetic fields of $B_0 = 0, 10^{10}, and 10^{12}$~G. We find that the magnetic field in the gain region does not become so large that it alters the global dynamics above the 10% level in the early post-bounce evolution. The turbulent kinetic energy of the fluid in the gain region is smaller in simulations with a strong initial magnetic field, but the exact amount of reduction is uncertain due to limitations of the methods for measuring turbulent kinetic energy. The structure of the field in the simulations quickly becomes a tangled mass of flux ropes as soon as convection begins, which leads to a large magnetic field contribution to the baroclinic vector that dominates over the hydrodynamic contribution. Although governed by very similar transport equations to the magnetic field, the fluid vorticity and magnetic field are always close to being randomly aligned at every stage of the evolution. The enstrophy, which is seen to be closely associated with the turbulent kinetic energy, is found to be reduced in simulations with a strong initial magnetic field supporting the inference that the magnetic field reduces the amount of turbulence in the fluid.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates magnetic field-fluid interactions in core-collapse supernovae using the ELEPHANT code with 15 and 20 solar-mass solar-metallicity progenitor stars and purely toroidal initial magnetic fields of 0, 10^10, and 10^12 G. The study finds that magnetic fields in the gain region do not alter global dynamics above the 10% level in early post-bounce evolution, though turbulent kinetic energy and enstrophy are reduced in simulations with stronger initial fields. The field rapidly becomes a tangled mass of flux ropes, and the magnetic contribution to the baroclinic vector dominates over hydrodynamics, while fluid vorticity and magnetic field remain randomly aligned throughout evolution.
AI.motivation: To understand how convective turbulent motion below the shock in core-collapse supernovae stretches and amplifies progenitor magnetic fields, and to explore the mutual interaction between magnetic fields and fluid dynamics, particularly the back-reaction of magnetic fields on fluid vorticity via the baroclinic vector and the resulting effects on turbulence.
AI.method: Using the ELEPHANT code, simulations of core-collapse supernovae are performed with solar-metallicity zero-age main sequence stars of 15 and 20 solar masses. Purely toroidal initial magnetic fields of B0 = 0, 10^10, and 10^12 G are imposed, and the evolution of magnetic field structure, turbulent kinetic energy, enstrophy, fluid vorticity, and baroclinic vector contributions are analyzed.
AI.result: The magnetic field in the gain region does not alter global dynamics above the 10% level in early post-bounce evolution. Turbulent kinetic energy and enstrophy are reduced in simulations with strong initial magnetic fields, though the exact reduction amount is uncertain due to measurement method limitations. The field rapidly becomes a tangled mass of flux ropes with a magnetic contribution to the baroclinic vector dominating over the hydrodynamic contribution. Fluid vorticity and magnetic field remain close to randomly aligned throughout evolution despite being governed by similar transport equations.
AI.conclusion: Strong initial magnetic fields reduce the amount of turbulence in the fluid in the gain region of core-collapse supernovae, as evidenced by reduced turbulent kinetic energy and enstrophy. However, the back-reaction of the magnetic field is not strong enough to alter global dynamics beyond the 10% level in the early post-bounce phase. The dominance of the magnetic contribution to the baroclinic vector and the rapid formation of tangled flux ropes characterize the magnetic field structure in these simulations.

title: Improving the Physical Interpretability of Gaussian Processes in Stellar Activity Modeling: A Study Case on Photometric Variability Among Stellar Clusters
summary:
Gaussian Processes (GPs) are widely used to model stellar variability in photometric surveys, but a statistically successful fit does not guarantee that the inferred hyperparameters correspond to physically meaningful stellar properties. This is especially important for young, active stars, whose TESS light curves contain evolving spots, harmonics, and non-sinusoidal variability. We use stellar rotation as a case study to examine when the period hyperparameter of a quasi-periodic GP can be interpreted as a physical rotation period. We introduce a regularized GP likelihood that reweights the covariance-complexity term in the marginal likelihood, reducing the tendency of unconstrained models to converge toward preferred but misleading solutions.
  We test this framework on 539 stars in IC2602, the Tucana-Horologium Association, Pisces-Eridanus, and GroupX, with independently reported and manually vetted rotation periods. This benchmark evaluates GP hyperparameter interpretability and automated period recovery with minimal human intervention. We compare regularized and unregularized models across several regularization strengths, λ, using literature agreement, sector-level diagnostics, and consistency across TESS sectors. Relative to the standard GP likelihood, regularization improves successful rotation-period recovery by an average of 7%. It also generally reduces the median absolute fractional deviation of periods across sectors, showing that the improvement is not limited to catastrophic failures but also mitigates smaller systematic errors.
  Regularization is particularly beneficial for non-sinusoidal or evolving modulation, where unconstrained GPs may recover harmonics or spurious timescales. These results show that likelihood regularization and cross-sector consistency are practical diagnostics for assessing when GP-based rotation periods are robust.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem that Gaussian Process hyperparameters, particularly the period parameter, may not correspond to physically meaningful stellar rotation periods despite statistically good fits. The authors introduce a regularized GP likelihood that reweights the covariance-complexity term to reduce convergence toward misleading preferred solutions, improving rotation period recovery by ~7% on average across 539 stars in several young stellar associations.
AI.motivation: Statistically successful GP fits to stellar variability do not guarantee physically interpretable hyperparameters. This is especially problematic for young, active stars whose TESS light curves exhibit evolving spots, harmonics, and non-sinusoidal variability, where the period hyperparameter may not correspond to the true rotation period.
AI.method: The authors introduce a regularized GP likelihood that reweights the covariance-complexity term in the marginal likelihood to discourage convergence toward preferred but misleading solutions. They test this across multiple regularization strengths (λ) on 539 stars from IC2602, Tucana-Horologium, Pisces-Eridanus, and GroupX using independently vetted rotation periods as ground truth, evaluating via literature agreement, sector-level diagnostics, and cross-sector consistency.
AI.result: Regularization improves successful rotation-period recovery by an average of 7% relative to standard GP likelihood and reduces the median absolute fractional deviation of periods across TESS sectors. Improvements are not limited to catastrophic failures but also mitigate smaller systematic errors, particularly for non-sinusoidal or evolving modulation where unconstrained GPs may recover harmonics or spurious timescales.
AI.conclusion: Likelihood regularization and cross-sector consistency serve as practical diagnostics for assessing when GP-based rotation periods are robust and physically meaningful, rather than merely statistically well-fit.

title: Photospheric index of geomagnetic activity
summary: Geomagnetic indices quantify the disturbances of the Earth's magnetic field. They form an important space weather and space climate record that tracks solar-terrestrial effects on the Earth. Although geomagnetic activity has its origins in the photospheric magnetic fields, the two have so far not been directly related. We develop a photospheric index of geomagnetic activity (PIGA) that measures the geoeffectiveness of the Sun based on photospheric magnetic field as presented in synoptic magnetograms. We construct the PIGA from synoptic magnetograms of Wilcox Solar Observatory by relating the equatorial and axial dipole components of the photospheric magnetic field to the geomagnetic Kp index by means of linear regression. PIGA captures well the evolution of the geomagnetic activity over the past 50 years at the resolution of solar rotation, having linear correlation of 0.71 with the geomagnetic Kp index. PIGA makes it straightforward to measure the geoeffectiveness of the Sun using the dominant structure of the global solar magnetic field. PIGA can for example be used to study the geoeffectiveness of the Sun using historical simulations or the predicted solar magnetic field. PIGA also allows to use observed geomagnetic activity as an additional constraint for the early magnetic field reconstructions of the solar magnetic field.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a Photospheric Index of Geomagnetic Activity (PIGA), a new index that directly relates photospheric magnetic fields (from Wilcox Solar Observatory synoptic magnetograms) to the geomagnetic Kp index using linear regression of equatorial and axial dipole components, achieving a 0.71 linear correlation over the past 50 years at solar-rotation resolution.
AI.motivation: Although geomagnetic activity originates from photospheric magnetic fields, the two have not been directly related before. The authors aim to bridge this gap by developing an index that measures the Sun's geoeffectiveness directly from photospheric magnetic field data.
AI.method: The authors construct PIGA by relating the equatorial and axial dipole components of the photospheric magnetic field (from Wilcox Solar Observatory synoptic magnetograms) to the geomagnetic Kp index via linear regression.
AI.result: PIGA captures the evolution of geomagnetic activity over the past 50 years at solar-rotation resolution, achieving a linear correlation of 0.71 with the Kp index.
AI.conclusion: PIGA enables straightforward measurement of the Sun's geoeffectiveness using the dominant global solar magnetic field structure, with applications in historical simulations, predicted solar magnetic fields, and constraining early solar magnetic field reconstructions.

title: Calculation of Field Line Slippage Rates in Coronal Simulations
summary: We present the Universal Slippage calculator (\texttt{USlip}), an extension of the Universal Fieldline Tracer (\texttt{UFiT}), that computes magnetic field line slippage rates from an input magnetic field defined on a structured grid. The slippage rate provides a local, physically grounded diagnostic of non-ideal evolution, directly quantifying departures from ideal frozen-in motion. We outline the theoretical formulation and describe an efficient numerical implementation. The method is validated against analytical solutions and applied to simulations using three coronal codes treating varying spatial scales, all of which are standard inputs for \texttt{USlip}. In all the examples considered, the slippage rate not only identifies where magnetic connectivity changes occur, but also accurately reproduces the observed direction of field-line slippage. The consistency of the results across analytical tests and multiple simulation platforms demonstrates that \texttt{USlip} is a robust and versatile tool for diagnosing three-dimensional reconnection in dynamically evolving systems.

AI.tldr: USlip is an extension of the Universal Fieldline Tracer that computes magnetic field line slippage rates from structured-grid magnetic field inputs, providing a local diagnostic of non-ideal evolution and reconnection. It is validated analytically and across three coronal simulation codes, accurately identifying both where and in what direction magnetic connectivity changes occur.
AI.motivation: To provide a robust, versatile, and physically grounded diagnostic tool for quantifying departures from ideal frozen-in motion in dynamically evolving magnetic systems, enabling identification and characterization of three-dimensional reconnection.
AI.method: The slippage rate is computed from a magnetic field defined on a structured grid via theoretical formulation and efficient numerical implementation. The method is validated against analytical solutions and applied to simulations from three coronal codes covering varying spatial scales.
AI.result: Across analytical tests and multiple simulation platforms, the slippage rate correctly identifies where magnetic connectivity changes occur and accurately reproduces the observed direction of field-line slippage, demonstrating robustness and versatility.
AI.conclusion: USlip is a reliable and general-purpose tool for diagnosing three-dimensional reconnection in dynamically evolving systems.
